claims.text: A fully homogenized equiatomic high-entropy alloy can provide a near-ideal random solid-solution baseline with minimal short-range order.
Controlled heat treatment can vary local chemical order while preserving overall alloy composition.
Heat-treatment-induced changes in local chemical order are accompanied by corresponding changes in lattice distortion.
Electron diffraction and atom probe tomography can detect or quantify local chemical ordering in concentrated alloys.
Electron diffraction or atom probe tomography can determine the magnitude of ordering-associated lattice distortion.
Local chemical ordering introduces spatial variations in lattice strain.
Increasing local chemical order raises activation barriers governing dislocation activity.
The higher dislocation barriers arise specifically from ordering-induced lattice strain.
Higher barriers increase lattice friction and reduce dislocation mobility.
Changes in short-range order can alter dislocation-slip behavior and deformation pathways.
Samples with greater local chemical order will have greater lattice distortion than the homogenized baseline.
Greater local chemical order will increase hardness relative to the homogenized, disordered baseline.
Greater local chemical order will increase yield strength relative to the homogenized, disordered baseline.
The increases in hardness and yield strength will be statistically significant beyond experimental uncertainty.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase solid solutions without precipitation or phase transformations under the processing and test conditions.
Conventional dislocation interactions may overlap with the ordering effect and make its magnitude uncertain.
A composition-matched, identically tested low-order baseline is an experimental control for isolating the effect of local chemical order.
Failure of the ordered samples to show a statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength would falsify the stated hypothesis.
